questions.questionText:
Cell Membranes & Fluid Mosaic Model:
(a) Describe the roles of phospholipids, cholesterol, and glycoproteins in the plasma membrane. [5 marks]
(b) Contrast facilitated diffusion with active transport across membranes. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Phospholipid bilayer provides hydrophobic barrier to water-soluble ions; cholesterol regulates membrane fluidity/mechanical stability across temperatures; glycoproteins act as cell-recognition antigens and hormone receptors [5].
(b) Facilitated diffusion is passive down a concentration gradient via channel/carrier proteins requiring no ATP; active transport pumps molecules against their gradient using ATP energy [3].

questions.questionText:
Enzyme Kinetics:
Explain how substrate concentration, pH extremes, and non-competitive inhibitors alter the shape of a Michaelis-Menten rate curve (V_max and K_m). [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Increasing [S] raises rate linearly until all active sites saturate at plateau V_max [2]. Extreme pH alters R-group ionisation breaking ionic/H-bonds and denaturing the active site [2]. Non-competitive inhibitors bind allosteric sites permanently changing active-site shape, lowering V_max without changing apparent K_m [2].

questions.questionText:
Protein Synthesis (Transcription & Translation):
Outline the sequence of events by which the base sequence of a gene on DNA produces a functional polypeptide on a ribosome. [8 marks]
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase binds promoter, unzips DNA H-bonds, and joins complementary RNA nucleotides (A-U, G-C) on the template strand forming pre-mRNA/mRNA [3]. Introns are spliced out and mRNA exits via nuclear pore to ribosome [1]. tRNAs carrying specific amino acids pair complementary anticodons to mRNA codons at P/A sites; peptidyl transferase forms peptide bonds as ribosome shifts codon-by-codon until a stop codon releases the folding polypeptide [4].

questions.questionText:
Mammalian Cardiac Cycle & Coordination:
Describe how the SAN, AVN, Bundle of His, and Purkinje fibres coordinate atrial and ventricular contraction during one heartbeat. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Myogenic SAN (pacemaker in right atrium wall) sends wave of excitation over both atria causing atrial systole [2]. Non-conducting fibrous ring delays impulse at AVN (~0.1 s) ensuring ventricles fill completely before contracting [2]. Excitation conducts rapidly down Bundle of His to apex and upward via Purkinje fibres so ventricles contract upward cleanly from apex to arteries [2].

questions.questionText:
Immunity & Vaccination:
Explain why measles vaccination confers long-term active artificial immunity, whereas injecting antivenom serum confers short-term passive artificial immunity. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Vaccines introduce harmless weakened/antigenic pathogens stimulating clonal B and T memory cells so secondary exposure triggers fast massive antibody synthesis (long-term active immunity) [3]. Antivenom supplies ready-made antibodies from another animal without activating the patient's B-memory cells; antibodies degrade over weeks giving short-term passive immunity [2].

questions.questionText:
Homeostasis — Osmoregulation by ADH:
Describe the negative feedback mechanism by which osmoreceptors, pituitary gland, ADH, and kidney collecting ducts respond when a marathon runner becomes dehydrated. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Dehydration lowers blood water potential -> detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors [1.5]. Posterior pituitary secretes more ADH into blood [1]. ADH binds collecting-duct receptors, triggering cAMP insertion of aquaporin water channels into luminal membranes [2]. More water reabsorbs osmotically into hypertonic medulla, yielding small volume of concentrated urine and restoring normal blood water potential [1.5].

questions.questionText:
Synaptic Transmission:
Explain how an action potential arriving at a presynaptic knob triggers excitatory depolarisation in a cholinergic postsynaptic neurone, and why transmission is unidirectional. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx makes synaptic vesicles fuse with presynaptic membrane releasing acetylcholine by exocytosis [2.5]. ACh diffuses across cleft, binds Na⁺-gated postsynaptic receptors generating an EPSP (action potential if threshold reached) before acetylcholinesterase recycles it [2.5]. Unidirectional because vesicles exist only in presynaptic knob and receptors only on postsynaptic membrane [1].

questions.questionText:
Photosynthesis — Light-Dependent Reactions (Z-Scheme):
Compare cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation in chloroplast thylakoids, listing reactants and products of each. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Non-cyclic uses PSII and PSI: photolysis of water splits H₂O → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ + ½O₂, electrons pass down ETC pumping H⁺ to drive chemiosmotic ATP synthesis, and reduce NADP⁺ → NADPH + H⁺ [4]. Cyclic uses only PSI: excited electrons cycle back down ETC generating ATP only (no photolysis, no O₂, no NADPH) [2].

questions.questionText:
Cellular Respiration — Chemiosmosis:
Explain how NADH and FADH₂ generated in the Krebs cycle drive ATP synthesis across the inner mitochondrial membrane. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: NADH/FADH₂ donate high-energy electrons to inner-membrane electron carriers; energy released as electrons pass down redox carriers actively pumps H⁺ from matrix into the intermembrane space creating an electrochemical proton gradient [3]. H⁺ ions diffuse back into matrix through ATP synthase stalked particles, rotating its catalytic head to combine ADP + Pᵢ → ATP, while oxygen receives final electrons forming water [3].

questions.questionText:
Genetics — Sex Linkage & Chi-Squared Test:
In humans, haemophilia is X-linked recessive (Xᴴ / Xʰ). A carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and an unaffected father (XᴴY) have children.
(a) Use a genetic diagram to show expected genotypes/phenotypes and probabilities. [4 marks]
(b) State why males express X-linked recessive conditions more frequently than females. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Gametes: Mother Xᴴ, Xʰ; Father Xᴴ, Y. Offspring: XᴴXᴴ (normal girl), XᴴXʰ (carrier girl), XᴴY (normal boy), XʰY (haemophiliac boy) -> 25% chance overall (50% of sons affected) [4].
(b) Males are hemizygous (XY) having only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele cannot be masked by a normal allele on Y [2].

questions.questionText:
Recombinant DNA & PCR:
Outline how the human insulin gene can be isolated, inserted into a bacterial plasmid vector, and verified using marker genes. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Extract pancreatic β-cell mRNA and convert to cDNA via reverse transcriptase [1.5]. Cut cDNA and plasmid with the SAME restriction endonuclease creating complementary sticky ends, anneal and seal with DNA ligase [2]. Transform E. coli via Ca²⁺ heat-shock; identify successful recombinant colonies using antibiotic-resistance / fluorescent GFP / lacZ blue-white replica-plating markers [2.5].

questions.questionText:
Natural Selection & Antibiotic Resistance:
Explain using Darwinian principles how overuse of antibiotics in clinics leads to widespread MRSA resistance in bacterial populations. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Pre-existing random DNA mutation creates a rare resistant bacterium in the population [1.5]. Antibiotic acts as a strong selective pressure killing susceptible bacteria while resistant mutants survive and reproduce rapidly by binary fission [2]. Over generations, the resistance allele frequency rises sharply across the population [1.5].

questions.questionText:
Transport in Plants — Xerophyte Adaptations:
Explain five structural adaptations of xerophytic plants (such as marram grass or cactus/acacia in arid Region V) that reduce excessive transpiration. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: 1. Thick waxy cuticle cuts cuticular evaporation. 2. Sunken stomata trap humid still air reducing water-potential gradient. 3. Rolled/needle leaves cut exposed surface area. 4. Leaf hairs (trichomes) maintain moist boundary layer. 5. Deep taproots or shallow widespread roots capture scarce rainfall [5].

questions.questionText:
Control of Blood Glucose:
Describe how pancreatic Islets of Langerhans (α and β cells), insulin, and glucagon maintain blood glucose homeostasis between meals and after a high-carbohydrate meal. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: High blood glucose: β-cells secrete insulin -> liver/muscle cells increase GLUT4 uptake, activate glycogenesis (glucose → glycogen), and boost respiration lowering blood sugar [3]. Low glucose: α-cells secrete glucagon -> activates glycogenolysis (glycogen → glucose) and gluconeogenesis in hepatocytes raising blood sugar [3].

questions.questionText:
Plant Growth Regulators — Gibberellins in Germination:
Outline the biochemical role of gibberellins (GA) in triggering barley seed germination when water enters the embryo. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Water imbibition activates embryo to synthesise gibberellin [1]. GA diffuses to aleurone layer and activates transcription/translation of hydrolytic enzyme genes including α-amylase [2]. α-Amylase diffuses into endosperm hydrolysing insoluble starch into soluble maltose/glucose, which fuels embryo respiration and radicle/plumule growth [2].

questions.questionText:
Biodiversity Sampling — Simpson's Index & Capture-Mark-Recapture:
(a) State the formula for Simpson's Index of Diversity (D) and interpret a value close to 1 vs 0. [3 marks]
(b) State three assumptions required for the Lincoln Index mark-release-recapture method to be valid. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) D = 1 - Σ(n/N)². Values near 1 indicate high species richness and evenness (stable resilient ecosystem); near 0 indicates low diversity [3].
(b) Marks do not harm survival or increase predation; marked individuals mix thoroughly back into population; population is closed (negligible births/deaths/migration between samples) [3].

questions.questionText:
Meiosis & Genetic Variation:
Explain how crossing over in Prophase I, independent assortment in Metaphase I, and random fertilisation generate genetic variation without altering chromosome number. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Crossing over at chiasmata exchanges alleles between non-sister chromatids of homologous bivalents creating recombinant chromosomes [2]. Independent assortment aligns maternal/paternal homologues randomly on Metaphase I equator (2ⁿ combinations) [2]. Fusion of any random sperm with any ovum further multiplies unique diploid zygotes while meiosis halves ploidy to preserve 2n across generations [2].

questions.questionText:
Nitrogen Cycle in Agriculture:
Identify the roles of (a) Rhizobium bacteria, (b) Nitrosomonas & Nitrobacter, and (c) Pseudomonas denitrifying bacteria in soil nitrogen cycling. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: (a) Rhizobium in legume root nodules fixes N₂ gas into ammonium/amino acids [2]. (b) Nitrosomonas oxidises NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ and Nitrobacter oxidises NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ under aerobic soil conditions (nitrification) [2]. (c) Denitrifiers convert nitrates back to atmospheric N₂ gas in waterlogged anaerobic soils [1].

questions.questionText:
Mammalian Gas Exchange — Chloride Shift:
Explain how most carbon dioxide from respiring tissues is transported in venous blood back to the lungs, including the role of carbonic anhydrase and the chloride shift. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: CO₂ enters erythrocytes where carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃, dissociating to H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ [2.5]. H⁺ binds haemoglobin forming haemoglobinic acid (buffering pH) [1.5]. HCO₃⁻ diffuses out into plasma while Cl⁻ ions move inward (chloride shift) to maintain electrical neutrality [2].

questions.questionText:
Genetic Screening & Gene Therapy:
Discuss two potential benefits and two ethical/technical challenges of somatic gene therapy for recessive genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Benefits: Targets root faulty CFTR gene restoring normal mucus clearance; relieves severe lifelong symptoms without repeated transplants [2.5]. Challenges: Short-lived non-dividing airway cells require repeated liposome/viral vector doses; viral vectors risk immune inflammation or insertional mutagenesis, plus high treatment cost [2.5].
